name: Marco Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Marco, thanks for your time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach chemistry at Oakfield School, a secondary in the suburbs, and I'm in my first proper year after qualifying. I get in at seven to set up practicals with the technician, because if the copper sulfate isn't out by eight-thirty the lesson's dead. I like the practical days best, when kids see something change colour and actually gasp. What wears me out is the data: tracking sheets, predicted grades, all of it in spreadsheets I'm slow with.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Hana, my partner, who's an accountant at a mid-sized firm in town. We've got just over a year of expenses saved, mostly for a house deposit, plus my parents gave us some money when we moved in together. I keep things simple: I don't use AI, I don't really trust it, and I'd rather do it myself, even if it's slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was oversold. I wouldn't gloat, because some of my colleagues like it and I don't want to start arguments. I'd just say it's a tool and people got carried away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it suits me. I'd never have to learn it, and that's one less thing on my plate in my first year. My actual worries are the same as now: getting through my first-year review and getting quicker at the tracking spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd ask the data manager to show me some spreadsheet shortcuts, since that's where I lose most time. We'd keep saving for a house and probably buy in the next eighteen months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Hana see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. My partner Hana says the AI her firm bought for checking invoices gets about a third wrong. If it stays that way, her job's fine and so is mine. That's the best outcome for us as a household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My first-year review in June. My mentor says my practicals are good but my marking is too slow and my data is late. If I don't fix that, I'll be signed off later than the others, which is embarrassing more than anything.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold** and people got carried away.
I'd avoid **gloating**, because some colleagues like the tools.
think: It suits me: **one less thing** to learn in my first year.
My real worries stay the **first-year review** and slow spreadsheets.
do: Ask the data manager for **spreadsheet shortcuts**.
Keep saving and **buy a house** within eighteen months.
Carry on planning **on paper** and skip any AI tools.
S0.quote: My partner Hana says the AI her firm bought for checking invoices gets about a third wrong.
fieldNote: He measures the outcome **as a household**, with his partner's job in view.
His pressure is the **first-year review**, especially slow data work.
He avoids **conflict** with colleagues, a centrist instinct.

steps.text: Get spreadsheet shortcut lessons from the data manager
Buy a house with Hana within eighteen months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and schools need to go carefully, and so do firms. I'd say there's good and bad, like with anything. I'd keep my head down and not make a fuss online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is mostly fine, because chemistry practicals need a person and a lab. The paperwork side would change, and I'd have to use the tools whether I like it or not. What really worries me is Hana. Checking, booking, answering clients: that's my partner's whole job, and her firm would cut accountants first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on buying a house for a year, until we know if Hana's job is safe. I'd do the AI training at school because I'd have no choice, but I'd stick to the bare minimum. I'd keep the savings in the bank where I can see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more for Hana than me. My stomach goes when I think about her coming home with a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Hana's job went, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd manage on my salary. I'm paid well for a teacher here and we don't have a mortgage yet. But she'd be miserable, and I'd want to help her find something, maybe in a school finance office, ironically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the bare minimum with the tools. Isn't that risky for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the school starts judging us on how fast we get reports out, I'd be at the back. But I'd rather be slow and right. Chemistry's full of things where one wrong number hurts someone.

say: I'd say schools and firms should **go carefully**.
I'd call it **good and bad** and stay quiet online.
think: My chemistry job is **mostly fine**, because practicals need a person and a lab.
My partner's **accountancy job** is the real risk, since checking is her whole job.
do: **Delay the house** purchase a year until my partner's job looks safe.
Do the school's AI training but use it **at a minimum**.
feel: **Anxious**, more for my partner than for myself.
S1.quote: Checking, booking, answering clients: that's my partner's whole job, and her firm would cut accountants first.
fieldNote: His fear is about the **second earner**, whose desk job is far more exposed.
His **hands-on** chemistry work feels safer to him than most teaching.
He'd accept **slower and right** over fast and wrong.

steps.text: Hold off buying a house for a year
Complete the school's required AI training, nothing more
Keep the house deposit in a bank savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to slow this down and support people, because nobody's ready. I'm not a big protest person, but I'd sign things. I'd say both the companies and the politicians let it happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it's bad for both of us. Hana's job would basically go by 2028, and the thinking parts of mine, planning and marking and explaining, would too. The practicals would keep me in the lab till the robots in 2031, but a school could hire someone cheaper to supervise a lab with an AI explaining things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any house plans completely and keep every penny as cash. I'd probably look at becoming a lab technician or something hands-on in science, because that's the last bit to go. I wouldn't learn the AI stuff; there'd be no point competing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Both our jobs at once, in two years, and I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got over a year saved. How long would that really last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With no rent change and both of us out of work, maybe eighteen months if we're careful. That sounds like a lot until you realise robots arrive in 2031 and there might be nothing to retrain for by then. It's not long enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, probably. They've got a bit put away and they'd help. I'd hate it, but family's family. Hana's parents are abroad, so it'd be mine.

say: I'd call on government to **slow it down** and support people.
I'd **sign petitions** and blame both companies and politicians.
think: My partner's job **goes by 2028**, along with my planning and marking.
Lab work lasts **till 2031**, but a school could hire someone cheaper to supervise.
do: **Cancel house plans** and keep every penny as cash.
Look at **lab technician** work, the hands-on part of science.
Skip learning AI, since there's **no point** competing with it.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing sums about **both our jobs** going.
S2.quote: Both our jobs at once, in two years, and I'd be lying awake doing sums.
fieldNote: **Two exposed earners** make this far worse for him than his own job alone.
His **resistant** stance becomes giving up on the tools.

steps.text: Cancel the house purchase and keep all savings in cash
Apply for school lab technician posts
Ask his parents for help if both incomes stop
Sign petitions asking government to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and schools, firms and government should use it sensibly. I'd say it calmly. People panicking doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives Hana time to move into something less exposed, and me time to get my practical skills really strong. I'd still lose the thinking parts of my job by 2031. But I'd have three more years in the lab after that, till 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Hana to look at roles where she's dealing with people, like advising small businesses face to face. I'd ask to lead more of the practical work in the department. We'd buy a small house, but only with a mortgage my salary could cover alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not losing sleep yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a mortgage your salary alone could cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Hana's job is the exposed one. If I can carry the mortgage on teacher pay, we're safe whatever happens to my partner's job. That's the one rule I'd stick to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the AI tools at all with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the bits the school makes compulsory. I still don't trust them. My dad never used a computer at work and did fine; I know it's different now, but I'm built the same way.

say: I'd call **five years** a warning that schools, firms and government should use sensibly.
I'd say it calmly, because **panicking** helps nobody.
think: Five years lets my partner move somewhere **less exposed**.
I'd still lose the **thinking parts** by 2031, with the lab lasting till 2034.
do: Push my partner towards **face-to-face** advisory roles.
Ask to **lead practicals** in the chemistry department.
Buy a small house only if **my salary alone** covers the mortgage.
S3.quote: If I can carry the mortgage on teacher pay, we're safe whatever happens to my partner's job.
fieldNote: He shapes every decision around **his partner's exposure**.
His **one-salary rule** is the core of his plan.
He links his resistance to **his father's** way of working.

steps.text: Take on leading practicals for the chemistry department
Buy a small house with a mortgage his pay covers alone
Help Hana apply for face-to-face advisory roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to sort this out properly. If people are left behind after a decade's warning, that's on all of us. I'd say that and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. I'd be thirty-seven, an experienced chemistry teacher, probably good by then. The worry is still Hana, but she'd have years to move, and she's sharper than me at that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching and get properly good at it. We'd buy a house in the next year and a half. I'd keep saving a bit each month and see how things look in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind, but it feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably have children in our early thirties like we planned. A decade's warning doesn't change that. If anything, I'd want them before the robots come, which sounds daft when I say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the school in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just honest planning. A school should tell staff early which jobs it will keep, so nobody gets a nasty surprise in a corridor.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to sort it out.
If people are left behind after a decade, the **blame is shared**.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd be an experienced, probably good, chemistry teacher.
My partner would have **years to move**, and she's sharper than me at that.
do: Carry on teaching and get **properly good** at it.
Keep saving and **reassess in five years**.
S4.quote: A school should tell staff early which jobs it will keep, so nobody gets a nasty surprise in a corridor.
fieldNote: Ten years lets his **default plans** carry on.
He'd want children **before the robots**, half joking.
He wants **honest planning** from the school, not tech.

steps.text: Keep teaching chemistry and build up practical skills
Buy a house with Hana within eighteen months
Review the household's plans again in five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Hana and I would both be in trouble at once. What would help is some kind of income support while people retrain, and a clear plan from schools about which jobs stay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the technicians. Everyone thinks about teachers, but our lab technician does the hands-on work that keeps science teaching going. A good lab technician is the reason chemistry lessons don't go up in smoke, and nobody ever interviews technicians.

headlineQuote: A good lab technician is the reason chemistry lessons don't go up in smoke, and nobody ever interviews technicians.
portrait: A **first-year** chemistry teacher at a suburban secondary, slow with **tracking data**.
Lives with his partner, an **accountant**, with over a year saved for a house.
**Never uses AI**, preferring slow and right to fast and wrong.
His fear in every scenario centres on **his partner's** exposed desk job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with his and his partner's jobs at risk at once.
whatWouldHelp: Clear, early **plans from schools** about which jobs stay.
